newsitem.title: USA: N.J. man guilty of murder in Megan's Law case.
newsitem.headline: N.J. man guilty of murder in Megan's Law case.

text.p: A New Jersey man was convicted Friday on charges he sexually attacked and murdered 7-year-old Megan Kanka, an attack that resulted in the so-called Megan's Law for convicted child molesters.

Jesse Timmendequas, 36, was found guilty of all eight charges against him including capital murder, for which the penalty ranges from a minimum of 30 years in prison without parole to death by injection.
He was impassive as the seven-woman, five-man jury delivered its jerdict. Megan's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, sighed and sobbed.

Judge Andrew Smithson of Mercer County Superior Court said the penalty phase of the trial before the same jury might begin June 9 or earlier. At that time, the defence is expected to argue there were mitigating circumstances surrounding the crime and in Timmendequas' childhood.

Timmendequas was accused of luring Megan Kanka to the bedroom of his house in Hamilton Township, New Jersey, on July 29, 1994, to see a puppy and then attacking and killing her. Testimony by the local medical examiner showed that the girl was battered, suffocated, raped and sodomized and that she had struggled with her attacker for as long as 15 minutes.
The crime touched off a public outcry because the girl's parents had not known that Timmendequas, who lived across the street, was a sex offender twice convicted in assaults on girls aged 7 and 5.

"This has been a terrible tragedy for the Kanka family and their community," President Clinton said in a statement in Washington. "Megan's family took their pain and helped guide the nation to adopt legislation that is going to protect other children from those who would harm them. We owe the Kanka family not only our sympathy but a debt of gratitude as well."

Megan's Law, adopted in New Jersey as the result of the Kankas' impassioned campaigning, originally required sex offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.

But a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public, and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court. Critics say Megan's Law violates the Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served their prison sentence.
Most other states now have similar laws, and Clinton last year signed a federal law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.
Testimony in Timmendequas' trial began early in May. But jury selection took almost three months before that because of the notoriety of the case and the law it engendered.

As a result of the publicity and defence arguments that the defendant could not get a fair trial, the jurors were chosen from neighbouring Hunterdon County and were bused 20 miles to the courthouse each day.

Timmendequas was charged in an eight-count indictment, the stiffest charge of which was intentional death, which carries the possiblity of the death penalty. The other charges were kidnapping, aggravated sexual assault and felony murder.
Two days after Megan's disappearance, Timmendequas led police to her body in a county park two miles from her home in the working-class suburb of Trenton.
The prosecution, led by chief prosecutor Kathryn Flicker, rested its case May 22 after 14 days of testimony. The chief defence attorney was Barbara Lependorf.
